The Lions are Coming

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
After months of speculation and rumour, the British and Irish Lions management confirmed that the long-planned for tour of the famous rugby union team to South Africa is on. The four-yearly Lions tours are the blue riband of rugby, the pinnacle of a player’s career and for their opponents, an opportunity to play on a world stage only surpassed for glory by the World Cup.

Set to run from 3rd July to 7th August, the tour had been in doubt due to concerns over Covid-19 restrictions and the likely impact of the games being played without spectators.

Several contingencies had been under consideration, including accepting an offer by the Australian Rugby Union to move the tour to Australia where sports are now being played to near-full houses. Another option was moving the tour to Britain, which unlike South Africa has an advanced Covid-19 vaccination programme underway and is likely to admit spectators to sporting events by May. The third option was to postpone the tour by a year. All three were rejected after pressure from players and the rugby public mounted to stick to the original plan.


Further information:
This is huge in terms of our tourism industry which has lost millions directly and indirectly though the shut down. In Carte Blanche’s tourism programme in early December (last year) just before the second wave there was huge optimism that the tourism industry was about to open up only to disappointed at a further crackdown. Tourvest’s German CEO spoke bout a loss of 1 million jobs.

The Lions tour New Zealand, Australia and South Africa every four years in rotation, backed up by tens of thousands of delirious fans who pack out stadiums with a sea of red and white to contrast the green and gold of Springbok supporters. This time, the games will be played to an eerie silence though television viewers, starved of live-action international sport for months, will watch the matches accompanied by fake crowd noise to rev up the atmosphere.

The first test, to be played at FNB Stadium on 24th July, will be South Africa’s first since its crushing victory over England in the 2019 World Cup final in Japan. The Lions players will be coming off the recently played 6 Nations championship while the Springboks will be looking to repeat their 2-1 victory in the 2009 series and remain at the top of world rugby. The climax of this tour was Morne’ Steyn’s 54 metre injury time penalty kick which pipped the Lions to a narrow defeat, handing South Africa its series win.

“The 2019 World Cup-winning flyhalf Handre Pollard said playing the Lions had been a dream since he was a youngster and the 2019 World Rugby Player of the Year and World Cup winner Pieter-Steph du Toit described the Lions as bigger than the World Cup because they only visited every 12 years.” (IOL)


Every Lions Tour is unique but none more so than this year’s, due to the impact of Covid-19. Warren Gatland says he has been working hard to ensure the players have a brilliant experience.
“One of the things I have spoken about is putting the players first in terms of things we can do in the bubble. How we keep them entertained and mentally stimulated,” he said.
“That is really important. It is going to be a challenge to keep the players entertained and we have lots of ideas coming to us, card nights, games nights, pool games, golf simulators and all different things.
“We need to alleviate some of the issues, such as the boredom that comes with been cooped up all the time. It is going to be a challenge but hopefully we can get that right.”

Carte Blanche will interview leading players and coaches, past and present, to give viewers a taste of the nerves and excitement of the tour build up. The tour will be the biggest sporting event South Africa will have hosted since the 2010 World Cup soccer tournament and is estimated to create up to 13 000 temporary jobs.

John: He’s been a massive talking point around every single braai and its funny every single person that has played with him or against him will have put his name down 3 months ago.
He has ability to be handle pressure does miss odd kick but he never drops his head move on to the next task.

Morne: I’m older one this time I was the younger one 2009 but now the guys call me OOM.

Frans Steyn: I think I must first get into the team. I am here to win // still a lot of rugby to be played before the first test.

John: He’s just got to score in the first five minutes. Its about getting his group back in the same rythmn they were 2 years ago in Tokyo.

metadata.Summary: After months of speculation and rumour, the British and Irish Lions management confirmed that the long-planned for tour of the famous rugby union team to South Africa is on. The four-yearly Lions tours are the blue riband of rugby, the pinnacle of a player’s career and for their opponents, an opportunity to play on a world stage only surpassed for glory by the World Cup. Set to run from 3rd July to 7th August, the tour had been in doubt due to concerns over Covid-19 restrictions and the likely impact of the games being played without spectators. Several contingencies had been under consideration, including accepting an offer by the Australian Rugby Union to move the tour to Australia where sports are now being played to near-full houses. Another option was moving the tour to Britain, which unlike South Africa has an advanced Covid-19 vaccination programme underway and is likely to admit spectators to sporting events by May. The third option was to postpone the tour by a year. All three were rejected after pressure from players and the rugby public mounted to stick to the original plan.
metadata.Further information: This is huge in terms of our tourism industry which has lost millions directly and indirectly though the shut down. In Carte Blanche’s tourism programme in early December (last year) just before the second wave there was huge optimism that the tourism industry was about to open up only to disappointed at a further crackdown. Tourvest’s German CEO spoke bout a loss of 1 million jobs. The Lions tour New Zealand, Australia and South Africa every four years in rotation, backed up by tens of thousands of delirious fans who pack out stadiums with a sea of red and white to contrast the green and gold of Springbok supporters. This time, the games will be played to an eerie silence though television viewers, starved of live-action international sport for months, will watch the matches accompanied by fake crowd noise to rev up the atmosphere. The first test, to be played at FNB Stadium on 24th July, will be South Africa’s first since its crushing victory over England in the 2019 World Cup final in Japan. The Lions players will be coming off the recently played 6 Nations championship while the Springboks will be looking to repeat their 2-1 victory in the 2009 series and remain at the top of world rugby. The climax of this tour was Morne’ Steyn’s 54 metre injury time penalty kick which pipped the Lions to a narrow defeat, handing South Africa its series win. “The 2019 World Cup-winning flyhalf Handre Pollard said playing the Lions had been a dream since he was a youngster and the 2019 World Rugby Player of the Year and World Cup winner Pieter-Steph du Toit described the Lions as bigger than the World Cup because they only visited every 12 years.” (IOL) Every Lions Tour is unique but none more so than this year’s, due to the impact of Covid-19. Warren Gatland says he has been working hard to ensure the players have a brilliant experience. “One of the things I have spoken about is putting the players first in terms of things we can do in the bubble. How we keep them entertained and mentally stimulated,” he said. “That is really important. It is going to be a challenge to keep the players entertained and we have lots of ideas coming to us, card nights, games nights, pool games, golf simulators and all different things. “We need to alleviate some of the issues, such as the boredom that comes with been cooped up all the time. It is going to be a challenge but hopefully we can get that right.” Carte Blanche will interview leading players and coaches, past and present, to give viewers a taste of the nerves and excitement of the tour build up. The tour will be the biggest sporting event South Africa will have hosted since the 2010 World Cup soccer tournament and is estimated to create up to 13 000 temporary jobs.
